# The problem for today

## My sleep report {.center}

I want a summary of the sleep survey on:

1. How much do students in each program sleep? (*Numbers*, Chapter 13)
2. When do they go to bed? (*Strings*, Chapter 14)
3. Can we make the chart readable? (*Factors*, Chapter 16)


<!-- r setup -->

::: {.cell context='setup'}

:::


<!-- webr setup -->

::: {.cell autorun='true'}
```{webr}
#| include: false
#| autorun: true
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyverse)
library(readr)

survey <- read.csv("data/sleep_survey_v2.csv", fileEncoding = "WINDOWS-1252")
bed_clean <- survey |>
  select(student_id, bedtime) |>
  mutate(bedtime_clean = str_to_lower(str_trim(bedtime))) |>
  separate_wider_delim(
    bedtime_clean,
    delim = " ",
    names = c("time", "ampm"),
    too_few = "align_start",
    too_many = "merge"
  )
program_summary <- survey |>
  filter(!is.na(sleep_hours)) |>
  group_by(program) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean_sleep = mean(sleep_hours)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    hours = mean_sleep %/% 1,
    minutes = round((mean_sleep %% 1) * 60),
    rank_least = min_rank(mean_sleep)
  )
```
:::



::: {.cell}
```{webr}

```
:::


::: {.callout-tip title="Not everything fits in this 80-minute lecture"}
I may leave some of the undiscussed functions or tools in an *appendix table* at the end of the slide deck. Each row will say what the tool does and which section of the chapter to read. You should definitely take a look at the text for more details.

# Part 1: Numbers

## Learning Objectives

| Step | Tool (Chapter 13) |
|--------|-----------------|
| Fix numbers typed as text | `parse_number()` |
| Count students | `count()`, `n()` |
| Transform columns | `pmin()`, `pmax()`, `%/%`, `%%`, `round()`, `cut()` |
| Rank programs | `min_rank()` |
| Summarize | `mean()`, `median()` |

## Making numbers: 

::: {.callout-note title="`parse_number()`"}
Numbers sometimes arrive as text, typically when data is imported. *readr* has two parsers:
- `parse_double()` for strings that are clean numbers
- `parse_number()` for strings with extra text around the number
:::


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
parse_double(c("1.2", "5.6", "1e3"))
parse_number(c("$1,234", "USD 3,513", "59%"))

# Imagine students typed their weekly work hours as text
parse_number(c("10 hours", "12h", "about 8"))
```
:::


::: {.callout-important title="Checkpoint"}
Do you see what these functions are trying to do?
:::

## Counting 

::: {.callout-note title="`count()`"}
This function gives a quick tally of how many rows have each value. Add `sort = TRUE` to see the biggest groups first.
:::


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
survey |> count(program)
survey |> count(favourite_drink, sort = TRUE)
```
:::


`count()` is a shortcut. The long way lets you compute extra summaries in the same step:


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
survey |>
  group_by(program) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean_sleep = mean(sleep_hours, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```
:::


::: {.callout-warning title="n() only works inside dplyr verbs"}
`n()` returns the size of the current group. Outside of `summarize()`, `mutate()`, or `filter()`, there is no "current group", so it fails.
- i.e. `survey |> n(program)` doesn't mean anything.
:::

## Recycling Vectors

When two vectors have different lengths, *R* recycles the shorter one by repeating it. That can quietly give wrong answers. Are the students in Arts or Business?


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
survey |>
  filter(program == c("Arts", "Business")) |>
  count(program)
```
:::


::: {.callout-warning title="Doesn't give you an error, just the wrong answer"}
*R* compares `program` with `"Arts", "Business", "Arts", "Business", ...` row by row. It does **not** ask "is the program Arts or Business?". You only get about half of the students.
:::

The fix is `%in%`, which you've seen in last lecture:


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
survey |>
  filter(program %in% c("Arts", "Business")) |>
  count(program)
```
:::


## A simpler example

:::{.callout-tip title="Live Exercise"}
Run the following code to test how *R* recycles vectors of values
:::


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
x <- c(1,2,3,4,5,6)
y <- c(1,2)
z <- c(1,2,3,4)

x*y
x*z
```
:::



## Maximum and Minimum

- `pmin()` and `pmax()` work **row by row** across vectors (the "p" is for parallel)
- `min()` and `max()` summarize **everything** into one value


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
df <- tribble(
  ~x, ~y,
  1,  3,
  5,  2,
  7, NA,
)

df |>
  mutate(
    pmin = pmin(x, y, na.rm = TRUE),
    pmax = pmax(x, y, na.rm = TRUE),
    min = min(x, y, na.rm = TRUE),
    max = max(x, y, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```
:::


::: {.callout-important title="Key idea"}
Every row gets the **same** answer from `min()` and `max()`: the smallest and largest value in both columns combined. Use `pmin()` and `pmax()` for a per-row answer.
:::

## Time: Hours and minutes

:::{.callout-note title="Modular Arithmetic"}
Division with a quotient and a remainder:
- `%/%` is integer division
- `%%` is the remainder
- E.g. `7%/%3=2` and `7%%3=1`.
:::



::: {.cell}
```{webr}
1:10 %/% 3
1:10 %% 3
```
:::


`sleep_hours = 6.7` means 6 hours and 42 minutes. Modular arithmetic splits it:


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
survey |>
  mutate(
    hours = sleep_hours %/% 1,
    minutes = round((sleep_hours %% 1) * 60),
    .keep = "used"
  )
```
:::


## Rounding

:::{.callout-note title="`round(x)`"}
This function rounds to the nearest integer. You can even add a `digits` argument that controls where to round, and this value `digits` can be negative!
:::


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
round(123.456)
round(123.456, 1)   # one digit
round(123.456, -1)  # round to the nearest ten
```
:::


Grades rounded to the nearest ten:


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
survey |>
  count(grade_tens = round(avg_grade, -1))
```
:::


::: {.callout-caution title="Always round down or up?"}
`floor()` always rounds down and `ceiling()` always rounds up. See the appendix.
:::

## Cutting numbers into ranges

:::{.callout-note title="`cut()`"}
This function chops a numeric vector into *bins* and returns a factor. You supply the break points. Give `labels` one *fewer* element than `breaks`.
:::


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
x <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 15, 20)
cut(x, breaks = c(0, 5, 10, 15, 20), labels = c("sm", "md", "lg", "xl"))
```
:::


::: {.callout-tip title="Open-ended bins"}
- Values **outside** the breaks become `NA`. Use `-Inf` and `Inf` as the outer breaks so nothing falls off the ends.
- Bins are right-closed by default, like `(5, 10]`. Pass `right = FALSE` to make them left-closed, like `[5, 10)`.
:::

## Using `cut()` to get labels

In last class, we made sleep groups with `case_when()`. `cut()` does the same job in one line:


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
survey |>
  mutate(
    sleep_group = cut(
      sleep_hours,
      breaks = c(-Inf, 6, 7.5, Inf),
      labels = c("Short", "Typical", "Long"),
      right = FALSE
    ),
    .keep = "used"
  ) |>
  count(sleep_group)
```
:::



## Ranking

:::{.callout-note title="`min_rank()`"}
This function gives the rank of each value. `1` is the smallest, unless you flip it with `desc()`.
:::


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
survey |>
  group_by(program) |>
  summarize(mean_sleep = mean(sleep_hours, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(
    rank_least = min_rank(mean_sleep),
    rank_most = min_rank(desc(mean_sleep))
  )
```
:::


- Which program sleeps the least?

## Summaries: mean or median?


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
survey |>
  summarize(
    mean_work = mean(work_hours_week),
    median_work = median(work_hours_week)
  )
```
:::


Why are they so different? Look at the distribution:


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
ggplot(survey, aes(x = work_hours_week)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2)
```
:::


::: {.callout-important title="Perhaps an explanation"}
Many students do not work at all, which drags the median down while a few heavy workers pull the mean up. When a distribution is **skewed**, maybe it's worth it to report both mean and median.
:::

## Back to answering the question


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
program_summary <- survey |>
  filter(!is.na(sleep_hours)) |>
  group_by(program) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean_sleep = mean(sleep_hours)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    hours = mean_sleep %/% 1,
    minutes = round((mean_sleep %% 1) * 60),
    rank_least = min_rank(mean_sleep)
  )

program_summary
```
:::



## Exercise 1

:::


::: {.cell exercise='ex_numbers'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_numbers
survey |>
  mutate(
    study_band = cut(

    )
  ) |>
  count(study_band)
```
:::

```{webr}
#| solution: true

```
:::



# Part 2: Strings (Words)


## Learning Objectives

| Step | Tool (Chapter 14) |
|------|-------------------|
| Build text from data | `str_c()` |
| Measure text | `str_length()` |
| Split one column into several | `separate_wider_delim()` |
| Tidy up capitals | `str_to_lower()`, `str_to_upper()` |


## Combining text: 

:::{.callout-note title="`str_c()`"}
This function takes any number of vectors and returns a character vector. It is similar to base *R*'s `paste0()`, but it follows tidyverse recycling rules.
:::


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
str_c("x", "y", "z")
str_c("Hello ", c("John", "Susan")) # notice how I have a space after 'Hello'?

df <- tibble(name = c("Flora", "David", "Terra", NA))
df |> mutate(greeting = str_c("Hi ", name, "!"))
```
:::


::: {.callout-important title="Missing values are contagious"}
Just like in arithmetic, if any input is `NA`, the result is `NA`. The fourth greeting is missing.
:::

## Piecing everything together

Using the `program_summary` from Part 1, this builds the labels for our chart:


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
program_summary |>
  mutate(label = str_c(program, ": ", hours, " h ", minutes, " min"))
```
:::


## Oh wait! What's the problem?

:::{.callout-warning title="Checkpoint with `bedtime`"}
Click `Run Code` and view the `bedtime` variable from the first 15 responses. And then look at the counts of different types of responses collected from the students. Can I get any meaningful results from this table?
:::


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
survey |>
  select(student_id, bedtime) |>
  head(15)

survey |>
  count(bedtime, sort = TRUE)
```
:::


- `11:30 PM`, `11:30 pm`, `11.30 pm`, `23:30`, `2330`...
- Some entries are not even times at all
- We need to clean this column before we can use it

## Length of a string

:::{.callout-note title="`str_length()`"}
This function counts the characters in each string. A missing value gives `NA`.
:::


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
str_length(c("a", "R for data science", NA))
```
:::


The long entries in `bedtime`:


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
survey |>
  filter(str_length(bedtime) > 10) |>
  count(bedtime, sort = TRUE)
```
:::


- Long entries are usually hedged answers (`around ...`) or words instead of times

## Splitting into columns

:::{.callout-note title="`separate_wider_delim()`"}
A time like `"11:30 pm"` has two pieces separated by a space. This function splits a column on a delimiter, with a new column per piece. You supply *names* for the new columns.
:::


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
#| error: true
survey |>
  select(student_id, bedtime) |>
  separate_wider_delim(
    bedtime,
    delim = " ",
    names = c("time", "ampm")
  )
```
:::


::: {.callout-warning title="It refuses to guess"}
`separate_wider_delim()` expects every string to split into the **same number** of pieces. Real data does not. The function **errors** rather than guessing, and the message tells you what to try.
:::

## Debug mode

`too_few = "debug"` and `too_many = "debug"` keep the result but add diagnostic columns, named after the input column:

- `bedtime_ok`: did this row split cleanly?
- `bedtime_pieces`: how many pieces it had
- `bedtime_remainder`: any leftover text


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
bed_debug <- survey |>
  select(student_id, bedtime) |>
  separate_wider_delim(
    bedtime,
    delim = " ",
    names = c("time", "ampm"),
    too_few = "debug",
    too_many = "debug"
  )

bed_debug |>
  count(bedtime_ok, bedtime_pieces)

bed_debug |>
  filter(!bedtime_ok) |>
  count(bedtime, bedtime_pieces, sort = TRUE)
```
:::


- **Too few** pieces: `11:30PM`, `2330`, `midnight`
- **Too many** pieces: `around 11 pm`, `no set time`, and entries with a stray space at the start

## Fixing it

Tidy first, then tell the function what to do:

- `str_trim()` removes stray spaces at the start and end
- `str_to_lower()` makes `PM`, `Pm` and `pm` the same
- `too_few = "align_start"` fills missing pieces with `NA` at the end
- `too_many = "merge"` glues the extra pieces onto the last column


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
bed_clean <- survey |>
  select(student_id, bedtime) |>
  mutate(bedtime_clean = str_to_lower(str_trim(bedtime))) |>
  separate_wider_delim(
    bedtime_clean,
    delim = " ",
    names = c("time", "ampm"),
    too_few = "align_start",
    too_many = "merge"
  )

bed_clean |>
  count(ampm, sort = TRUE)
```
:::


## Putting the pieces together

Use `str_c()` to rebuild one standard bedtime. We only do it when `ampm` is really `am` or `pm`:


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
bed_std <- bed_clean |>
  mutate(
    bedtime_std = case_when(
      ampm %in% c("am", "pm") ~ str_c(time, " ", str_to_upper(ampm))
    )
  )

bed_std |>
  head(10)

bed_std |>
  count(bedtime_std, sort = TRUE)
```
:::


- Rows we cannot trust remain as `NA`

## How far did we get? {.smaller}

| Problem | Solved today? |
|---------|---------------|
| Capital letters (`PM`, `Pm`, `pm`) | Yes: `str_to_lower()` |
| Stray spaces | Yes: `str_trim()` |
| `11:30 pm` becomes `11:30 PM` | Yes: `separate_wider_delim()` and `str_c()` |
| Glued times (`11:30pm`, `12:00AM`) | **No** |
| Different separators and missing minutes (`11.30 pm`, `11 pm`) | **Partly**: they split, but are not in one format |
| Hedged answers (`around 11`, `~11:30 pm`) | **No** |
| 24-hour (`23:30`, `2330`) and no AM/PM (`11:30`) | **No** |
| `midnight`, `idk`, blank | **No** |

## Foreshadowing

::: {.callout-note title="Next week"}
We need a way to describe a **pattern** instead of an exact string. That is what regular expressions do (Chapter 15). Roughly 4 in 10 bedtimes are still unreadable after today.
:::

![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-9_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-35-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::

# Part 3: Factors


## Can we make the chart readable?

Here is what the pipeline gives us without any work:


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
program_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_sleep, y = program, fill = program)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.25))) +
  labs(
    title = "Average sleep by program",
    x = "Hours per night", y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```
:::


- Programs are in **alphabetical** order, which tells me nothing

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
A *factor* is how R stores a categorical variable that has a fixed set of possible values, which is called *levels*. *Factors* let you choose the order.
:::

## Creating a factor

:::{.callout-note title="`factor()`"}
Strings sort alphabetically (in default), which is rarely what you want. Start with a list of valid levels, then pass it to `factor()`:
:::


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
month_levels <- c(
  "Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun",
  "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"
)

x1 <- c("Dec", "Apr", "Jan", "Mar")
sort(x1)
sort(factor(x1, levels = month_levels))

# A typo
x2 <- c("Dec", "Apr", "Jam", "Mar")
factor(x2, levels = month_levels)
```
:::


::: {.callout-warning title="Silent NA"}
Any value that is **not** in `levels` silently becomes `NA`. There is no warning. Always check the result.
:::

## Reordering levels

:::{.callout-note title="`fct_reorder()`"}
This function `fct_reorder(f, x)` orders the levels of `f` by the values in `x`. It is perfect for plots.
:::



::: {.cell}
```{webr}
program_summary |>
  mutate(program = fct_reorder(program, mean_sleep)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_sleep, y = program, fill = program)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.25))) +
  labs(
    title = "Average sleep by program",
    x = "Hours per night", y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```
:::


- The program that sleeps the least is at the bottom, the most at the top

## Reordering by hand

:::{.callout-note title="`fct_relevel()`"}
The "sleep groups" from Lecture 8 are *text*, so a plot puts them in alphabetical order. `fct_relevel()` lets you list the levels in the order you want.
:::


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
sleep_groups <- survey |>
  filter(!is.na(sleep_hours)) |>
  mutate(
    sleep_group = case_when(
      sleep_hours < 6    ~ "Short",
      sleep_hours <= 7.5 ~ "Typical",
      sleep_hours > 7.5  ~ "Long"
    )
  )

# Alphabetical
sleep_groups |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sleep_group)) +
  geom_bar()

# In the order we choose
sleep_groups |>
  mutate(sleep_group = fct_relevel(sleep_group, "Short", "Typical", "Long")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sleep_group)) +
  geom_bar()
```
:::



## Renaming levels

:::{.callout-note title="`fct_recode()`"}
This function can be used to rename a *level*. The syntax is `new name = "old name"`. Also, *levels* you do not mention stay the same.
:::



::: {.cell}
```{webr}
survey |>
  filter(!is.na(favourite_drink)) |>
  mutate(drink = fct_recode(favourite_drink, "Soda" = "Pop")) |>
  count(drink)
```
:::



## Merging levels

:::{.callout-note title="`fct_collapse()`"}
This function can combine levels and put them into groups. In this case, we want to group the drinks by how much caffeine they usually contain:
:::


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
survey |>
  filter(!is.na(favourite_drink)) |>
  mutate(
    caffeine = fct_collapse(
      favourite_drink,
      Strong = c("Coffee", "Energy drink"),
      Mild = c("Tea", "Pop"),
      None = "Water"
    )
  ) |>
  count(caffeine)
```
:::


::: {.callout-tip title="A lookup table is better"}
Typing groupings by hand is fine for five drinks. With many levels, you would use a lookup table with the caffeine amounts instead. That is a **join**, in Lecture 11.
:::

## The finished chart


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
program_summary |>
  mutate(
    program = fct_reorder(program, mean_sleep),
    label = str_c(hours, " h ", minutes, " min")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_sleep, y = program, fill = program)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), hjust = -0.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.25))) +
  labs(
    title = "Average sleep by program",
    x = "Hours per night", y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```
:::


- **Numbers** gave us the averages, the hours and minutes
- **Strings** gave us the label
- **Factors** gave us the order

## Numbers: other tools (i) {.smaller}

| Tool | What it does | Tiny example | Read the section on |
|------|--------------|--------------|---------------------|
| `count(..., wt = )` | A weighted count: a sum of another column | `count(program, wt = study_hours_week)` | Counts |
| `sum(is.na(x))` | Counts the missing values | `sum(is.na(sleep_hours))` | Counts |
| `n_distinct()` | Counts the unique values. Does every student appear once? `NA` counts as a value unless `na.rm = TRUE` | `n_distinct(student_id)` | Counts |
| `floor()`, `ceiling()` | Round down / up. No `digits` argument, so scale first | `floor(123.456)` | Rounding |

| Tool | What it does | Tiny example | Read the section on |
|------|--------------|--------------|---------------------|
| `sd()`, `IQR()` | Spread: standard deviation, and the width of the middle half | `sd(sleep_hours, na.rm = TRUE)` | Spread |
| `quantile()` | Any percentile of a vector | `quantile(x, 0.9)` | Minimum, maximum, and quantiles |
| `log()`, `log2()`, `log10()` | Logarithms. Each +1 on `log2()` means the value **doubled** | `log2(c(1, 2, 4, 8))` | Logarithms |

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
